supportedClaims: Kumasi association, drill ancestry and commonly described language practices.

researchSources.title: The Native: Sounds From This Side, Asakaa Drill

researchSources.title: Pan African Music: Reggie Osei, Asakaa Drill

researchSources.title: Dodzi K. Aveh: The Woo Dance vs Kete

candidates.researchRationale: Historical scene and production descriptions do not establish sufficient predicates in current GI evidence. Keep recognition separate from construction.

research.definition: Asakaa is a Kumasi-associated Ghanaian hip-hop scene and musical practice drawing on drill while articulating local identities and production choices. Its boundaries are contested; it is not a universal synonym for Ghanaian rap.
research.musicalAncestry: Specialist descriptions connect US and UK drill with Ghanaian hip-hop and hiplife influences. Artist and producer accounts stress local production and rhythmic practices rather than translation alone.
research.requiredParentGenres: Hip-Hop is the descriptive ancestry. The reviewed sources do not establish a machine-testable parent-Genre conjunction sufficient to identify every Asakaa recording.
research.existingStyleRelationships: Drill is a substantial relationship. Trap and hiplife influences are descriptive; a Drill tag is neither a complete definition nor a sufficient construction predicate.
research.sceneRelationship: The Kumasi collective/scene is central to historical accounts, including Kumerica and local Saka usage. Current GI has no researched Asakaa-scene identity or per-recording affiliation evidence.
research.countryRelationship: Ghana is the historical scene association, not a proved nationality or birthplace requirement for every participant or recording. Reggie explicitly describes the practice as open beyond Ghana.
research.cityRelationship: Kumasi is the documented scene origin. The sources do not make current residence, birth in Kumasi, or an album artist location a necessary or sufficient recording-level condition.
research.languageRelationship: Twi, English and local Saka appear in artist accounts. Language use cannot be reduced to a required Twi tag; multilingual and collaborative practices undermine such a shortcut.
research.emergencePeriod: Accounts place drill uptake in the late 2010s, with a major visibility increase around 2020. Reggie describes interest in drill in 2019.
research.eraRequirement: Descriptive history only. A release-year cutoff is not a researched musical requirement, and GI dates are not qualified era evidence.
research.geographyRequirement: Scene affiliation matters descriptively; nationality, city and country tags are not equivalent to affiliation. No universally sufficient geographic condition is established.
recognitionAliases: No additional recognition aliases approved. Ghanaian Drill is a descriptive comparison, not an asserted canonical equivalence.
research.sufficientEvidence: No defensible deterministic sufficient condition is established in the qualified SC-1 fact vocabulary. An explicit canonical Asakaa tag may be recognized by Cleanup; it does not establish an inference rule.
insufficientEvidence: Ghana plus Hip-Hop plus Drill, individually or together.
Twi, a Kumasi location, a 2020s year, or artist membership without recording-level evidence.
Vibe/community tags, weighted agreement, or alias text not qualified by GI.
falsePositives: Other Ghanaian hip-hop or drill mistaken for Asakaa.
A non-Asakaa recording by an artist associated with the scene.
A collaboration classified from the featured or album artist location alone.
disqualifyingCases: For any future scene-affiliation predicate, explicit contradictory recording affiliation would require review; absent scene evidence is missing, not a contradiction.
An independently established non-drill recording would contradict a future rule that explicitly requires drill; the sources do not authorize that predicate universally.
Unknown/featured artist role cannot prove a required main-artist binding.
researchGaps: No formal recording-level membership criteria or sufficiency theorem in the reviewed sources.
Local rhythmic/production traits lack validated typed evidence in GI.
Scene identity, participation and artist roles are not retained as qualified facts.

candidates.researchRationale: Illustrative artist histories and localized drill descriptions do not authorize a country-plus-genre shortcut.

research.definition: Kenyan Drill describes localized drill practice within Kenyan hip-hop. Buruklyn Boyz are prominent documented participants, but one group does not define the whole scene or every recording.
research.musicalAncestry: Hip-hop with UK drill influence is documented in artist interviews. Nairobi popular music includes Genge, Kapuka and Gengetone, which are not interchangeable with Kenyan Drill.
research.requiredParentGenres: Hip-Hop is descriptive ancestry. Hip-Hop alone, or with a generic Drill label, is not sufficient; no universal computable parent rule was established.
research.existingStyleRelationships: UK drill is a documented influence; heavy bass and sparse rhythmic descriptions are not validated GI audio predicates. Drill labels do not establish Kenyan scene participation.
research.sceneRelationship: Local scene identity and practice matter. Interviews illustrate Buruklyn Boyz and Buruburu, but do not prove that affiliation with one group or neighborhood defines all Kenyan Drill.
research.countryRelationship: Kenya describes localization and scene context. Citizenship, birthplace and the album artist country are not sufficient track-level evidence.
research.cityRelationship: Nairobi and Buruburu are prominent in the reviewed artist accounts. A city or neighborhood requirement would overgeneralize these examples to an entire Style.
research.languageRelationship: English, Sheng and Kiswahili are documented. Ajay discusses Swahili as an artistic choice; no single language is established as universally necessary.
research.emergencePeriod: Reviewed accounts describe UK drill listening from 2016, group formation in 2019, and wider visibility in 2020–2021. These are artist/scene histories, not release-date gates.
research.eraRequirement: Descriptive only; neither a release year nor an artist debut date proves Style.
research.geographyRequirement: Kenyan scene localization is descriptive. No sufficient geographic predicate is established; residence or nationality is not recording-level affiliation.
recognitionAliases: Kenya Drill is an existing built-in recognition alias; no new alias is registered by this research dataset.
research.sufficientEvidence: No defensible deterministic sufficient condition is established using qualified SC-1 semantic facts. Explicit Kenyan Drill recognition is supported independently by Cleanup.
insufficientEvidence: Kenya plus Hip-Hop plus Drill, including a Nairobi artist address.
Swahili/Sheng or a neighborhood name without localized recording evidence.
Artist reputation, violence/protest themes, or a generic drill audio description.
falsePositives: Genge, Kapuka, Gengetone or other Kenyan rap classified as drill.
A non-drill recording by a drill-associated performer.
A foreign drill recording classified from a featured Kenyan artist or album-artist association.
disqualifyingCases: A proved non-drill recording would contradict a future rule explicitly requiring drill; mere absence of a Drill tag is only missing evidence.
Featured/unknown artist association cannot satisfy a main-artist requirement.
Contradictory recording-level scene evidence would require review; no universal exclusion by nationality, language or lyrical theme is asserted.
researchGaps: No general recording-level definition supplying necessary and sufficient predicates.
No validated typed drill-production evidence or Kenyan-scene participation contract.
Interviews are illustrative cases, not population-wide membership tests.

researchSources.access: Abstract/repository page only; full download unavailable

researchSources.title: Korea University: local Korean hip-hop scenes thesis

researchSources.title: Hae-kyung Um: Korean hip-hop and cultural reterritorialisation (2013)
supportedClaims: Abstract examines resistance, border crossing and localization, not a necessary-and-sufficient tag rule.

candidates.researchRationale: A transnational hip-hop field cannot be reduced to nationality, language, residence or an unqualified scene label.

research.definition: Korean Hip-Hop is a historically localized hip-hop field with underground, commercial and transnational practices. Nationality and Korean-language vocals are not interchangeable with participation in this field.
research.musicalAncestry: Hip-hop ancestry is clear. Research discusses localization, authenticity, resistance and reterritorialisation rather than a uniform sonic subtype.
research.requiredParentGenres: Hip-Hop is descriptive ancestry. A Hip-Hop tag cannot distinguish the Korean field; no sufficient canonical parent conjunction is established.
research.existingStyleRelationships: The field contains multiple rap/hip-hop practices and production approaches. No single existing Style relationship is established as required for every recording.
research.sceneRelationship: Underground networks and local scenes are documented, including activity beyond Seoul. Current GI has no qualified canonical Korean-hip-hop scene-participation fact.
research.countryRelationship: South Korea is the historical field association. Research includes transnational participants; ethnicity, citizenship and birthplace cannot be treated as sufficient or universal requirements.
research.cityRelationship: Seoul is prominent in fieldwork, while local-scene research includes Gunsan, Gwangju, Busan and Jangsu. No Seoul-only or single-city rule is defensible.
research.languageRelationship: Korean is common, but multilingual practice includes English and other languages. Korean lyrics alone also fail to distinguish hip-hop from other music.
research.emergencePeriod: Research situates localization and mainstream presence in the 1990s, with underground institutions developing later in that decade. These dates describe history, not track-level eligibility.
research.eraRequirement: Descriptive only. No release-era cutoff is asserted.
research.geographyRequirement: Scene/cultural participation is descriptive and transnational. Country/location without proved recording association and artist role is insufficient.
recognitionAliases: khip-hop is the researched recognition alias; k-hiphop is recognized by existing normalized lookup. This dataset does not change aliases.
research.sufficientEvidence: No defensible deterministic sufficient condition is established in qualified SC-1 semantic facts. An explicit Korean Hip-Hop value is recognition, not a new inferred Style.
insufficientEvidence: South Korean artist location plus Hip-Hop.
Korean language plus Hip-Hop, or Korean nationality alone.
K-pop marketing, a Korean featured artist, Seoul residence or an artist-level tag attached to every recording.
falsePositives: Korean-language pop containing a rap passage mistaken for hip-hop field membership.
A non-hip-hop recording by a Korean hip-hop performer.
A transnational collaboration classified solely from one featured performer or album artist.
disqualifyingCases: A recording independently established outside hip-hop would contradict a future explicit Hip-Hop requirement; absent genre metadata is missing evidence.
A location attached to an unknown/featured role cannot satisfy main-artist evidence.
Nationality, English vocals, diaspora or a non-Seoul location are not asserted disqualifiers.
researchGaps: Academic accounts explain field boundaries but supply no deterministic recording classifier.
GI lacks qualified scene participation and track-level artist-role contracts.
No universal language, country, city or existing-Style predicate is supported.
